title-group.article-title: Metals and Geochemical Indexes in Sediments of a Karstic Coastal Tropical Lagoon: Evaluating the Ecological Risk in Celestun, Yucatan, Mexico

abstract.p: Celestun is one of the most socio-environmentally important lagoons in Yucatan, Mexico, although it is vulnerable to contamination from in situ activities and to contaminants transported and released by the submarine groundwater discharges, mainly in the northern part of the lagoon. These contaminants, like metals, can accumulate in the sediments of the coastal lagoons and could eventually represent an ecological risk, thus, this research evaluate the enrichment factor, the geoaccumulation index and the ecological risk index to evaluate the environmental status of the lagoon. Sediments samples were collected during the main hydrological seasons, dry, rainy and Nortes, in selected sites. Results shown that metals distribution are related to (1) submarine groundwater discharges, (2) co-transport with fine materials in the rainy and Nortes season, and (3) in situ inputs from urban wastewater and agriculture. Cd, As and Sn were enriched in dry, rainy and Nortes season, going from minor to mildly sever enrichment, also, the geoaccumulation index indicated a minor to highly contaminated status, but the ecological risk was low. Metals are enriched and accumulating in the sediments, and although they represent a low ecological risk nowadays, this could change in the future as result of the economic development increase, that will release more wastewater and solid wastes that potentially could affect fisheries and human health.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: For centuries humans populations have benefited from the ecosystemic services provided by coastal areas, from food to materials and recreational opportunities (Mehvar et al. 2018). Today, approximately 40% of the global population resides within 100 km to the coast (Ávila-Foucat and Espejel 2020). However, unsustainable socioeconomic development has led to environmental degradation and has significantly affect the coastal systems (Figueroa-Zavala et al. 2015).

Coastal lagoons are particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic physical and chemical alterations (Barragán and Borja 2012) often driven by land use changes and inadequate waste management. Moreover, lagoon hydrodynamics can promote the accumulation of anthropogenic contaminants in the sediments (Arcega-Cabrera et al. 2014) posing risks to the benthic communities. Monitoring sediment-bound contaminants, such as metals, provides insight into environmental and serves as an early warning for potential human health risks (Arcega-Cabrera and Fargher 2016; Arcega-Cabrera et al. 2023) especially through fish consumption (Castañeda-Chávez et al. 2017).

To assess contamination and ecological risk defined as the likelihood of harm to plants, animals, and ecosystems from being exposed to one or more environmental stressors, Wang et al. (2015) developed a series of geochemical indexes to evaluate the potential contamination and the environmental risk, that allows to compare the increase in time of metals in sediments and contributes to develop mitigation strategies (Devanesan et al. 2020).

In Yucatan karst aquifer, the groundwater serves as a conduit for transporting contaminants from inland to coastal zones (Pérez-Ceballos et al. 2012, 2022; Arcega-Cabrera et al. 2021). Notably, only 4% of the wastewater in the state is treated, and local sources (urban and industrial) often rely on inefficient septic tanks and lack formal waste management programs. Consequently, metals from untreated and decomposing solid waste are likely entering coastal lagoons and accumulating in sediments (Robledo-Ardila et al. 2023, 2024).

The four main productive activities in the Celestún Lagoon, Yucatan, are fishing, ecotourism, commerce, and services. They are the economic pillars of the municipality, making up approximately 80% of the residents’ income (Casais Molina et al. 2015). Since fishing is a primary livelihood in this lagoon, therefore, making it essential to evaluate potential contamination and environmental risk to safeguard both ecosystems and human health. Metals from submarine groundwater discharges and local anthropogenic sources may be accumulating at levels that, while currently posing low ecological risk, could become significant under future scenarios of intensified development.

This study investigates metal distribution in Celestun Lagoon (CL), a site of high socioeconomic and ecological importance. CL is designated Biosphere Reserve and RAMSAR due to its endemic species, ecosystem services and mangrove coverage (Herrera-Silveira 1994; Casais Molina et al. 2015). The lagoon exhibits estuarine dynamics, receiving both ocean input and groundwater discharge, primarily in the north, resulting in a salinity gradient from north to south (Herrera-Silveira 1994; González et al. 2008).

Given the (a) the lagoon’s socioeconomic value, (b) its hydrological connectivity with the aquifer, (c) ongoing local activities and (d) near absence of wastewater treatment in the region, it is imperative to assess the ecological risk posed by metal accumulation. To this end, we apply geochemical indices- geoaccumulation index (Igeo), enrichment factor (EF) and ecological risk index (ER)-to evaluate the potential impact of sediment-bound metals on the lagoon´s ecosystem.

sec.title: Study Area
sec.p: Celestun Lagoon (CL) is located in the northwest side of the Yucatan Peninsula, between the 20° 45′ y 20° 58′ N and 90° 25′ W (Hardage et al. 2022; Herrera-Silveira 1994)). CL is protected from the adyacent sea by several sand barriers and exhibits a distinct salinity gradient characterized by two predominant zones. The inner region (northern part of the lagoon) displays salinity levels ranging from 5 to 12 PSU, primarily due to submarine groundwater discharges (SGD) ocurring in the northern and central areas. In contrast, the southern region shows salinity values around 30 PSU (Herrera-Silveira 1994). Celestun is designated as a RAMSAR site and features extensive mangrove coverage. The primary economic activities are fishing and tourism, although agriculture and livestock production have increase significantly in recent years (Casais Molina et al. 2015).

sec.title: Sampling and Metal Analysis
sec.p:
Surface sediment samples (c.a. 1–3 cm depth-11 samples in total) were collected in rainy (August 2023), Nortes (October 2023) and dry (May 2024) seasons from selected sites within CL (Fig. 1). Site selection was based upon salinity gradient (from north to south), vicinity to anthropogenic sources and/or submarine groundwater discharges. Samples were collected following the methods by Loring and Rantala (1992), we use a composite sample composed of three subsamples collected one meter apart and subsequently homogenized in a single container. Samples were refrigerated, freeze dried and sieve (500 mm mesh). Metals extraction was performed according to the methods of Loring and Rantala (1992) and Arcega-Cabrera et al. (2014) followed by microwave digestion using the Environmental Protection Agency method (EPA 3052 MF 100-T16).Fig. 1
Sampling sites and land use in Celestun lagoon, Yucatan, Mexico

Metal concentrations were analyzed using an Atomic Absorption Espectophotometer Annalyst 800 coupled with air/acethylene flame, graphite furnace, and hydride generator. Analytical quality of analysis was ensured by the Standard Reference Material SRM 1646a Estuarine Sediment. Mean percentage recovery was, 97.93%, 90.50% and 98.5% for As, Cd and Sn respectively. Detection limit for these elements was 0.0013 µg/g 0.0020 µg/g and 0.0003 mg/g from As, Cd and Sn respectively. The remaining elements percentage recovery and detection limit can be consulted in Table 3 (supplementary material).

sec.title: Geochemical Indexes
sec.p: These indexes were obtained according to Wang et al. (2015) as follows.

Background levels used for EF and Igeo were the typical concentrations (mg/kg) of heavy metals in the Earth’s crust as cited by Taylor and McLennan (1995) and McLennan (2001). These values were used to normalize the concentration of every given metal. For the case of ER, biological toxicity factor and background reference values were taken from Hakanson (1980). These background levels were also used by Wang et al. (2015).
With the purpose of highlighting the potential risk from metals in sediments, results, discussion and conclusions sections will focus mainly on metals that indicate a risk to the ecosystem.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Data was explored for distributional properties and homogeneity of variances. Normality was tested with a Shapiro–Wilks (95% confidence) test, and variance homogeneity was evaluated with Levene’s test. Data showed non-parametric distribution thus Kruskal–Wallis was used to test for spatial and temporal differences (p < 0.05). All analysis and graphical outputs that allow robust visualization were performed using OriginLab Pro 2019.

sec.title: Screening Quick Reference Tables (SQuiRTs)
sec.p: In this study, we employed the NOAA Screening Quick Reference Tables (SQuiRTs-Buchman 2008) as a preliminary screening tool to evaluate metal contamination levels in sediment samples.

The measured concentrations of metals such as arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), zinc (Zn), nickel (Ni), tin (Sn), aluminum (Al), and manganese (Mn) in Celestun Lagoon sediments were compared against the relevant sediment benchmarks provided in the SQuiRTs. Instances where contaminant concentrations exceeded the SQuiRTs thresholds were flagged as potential indicators of ecological or toxicological concern. Thus, results, discussion and conclusions sections will focus on metals surpassing SQuiRTs.

sec.title: Mapping
sec.p: The maps were made with the ArcMap 10.8 software, where the classification of each index is represented. In the case of sites with concentration < LD, the detection limit value was used to calculate the index, and it will be presented in the map.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Metal concentrations during the dry, rainy, and Nortes seasons are presented in Table 1 (Supplementary Material). Arsenic (As) and cadmium (Cd) exceeded the thresholds established in the SQuiRTs across all seasons, indicating a potential toxicological risk to the early stages of aquatic biota. In contrast, the other analyzed metals remained below the SQuiRTs thresholds, therefore discussion will be focused on metals exceeding SQuiRTs thresholds. Seasonal variation of metals is presented in box plots (Figs. 1 to 11 at Supplementary Material).

Spatial analysis (Table 2, Supplementary Material) showed significant differences in nickel (Ni), zinc (Zn), and tin (Sn). Ni and Sn reached higher concentrations during the dry season, indicating inputs from localized anthropogenic sources such as urban and industrial wastewater. Sn is likely associated with antifouling paints used in boat maintenance (Fujita et al. 2015; Telegdi et al. 2016). Zn concentrations were higher during the rainy season, suggesting an influence from submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) and surface runoff (Arcega-Cabrera et al. 2014; Kantún-Mazano et al. 2018).

Seasonal variation was also significant for Al, Mn, As, and Sn, with higher concentrations observed during the dry season. This pattern reflects reduced hydrological activity and limited water flushing during that period, conditions that favor the sedimentation of fine particles and the accumulation of contaminants.

Enrichment factor (EF) analysis (Table 4, Supplementary Material; Fig. 2) indicated minor to severe enrichment for Cd, As, and Sn, consistent with chronic anthropogenic inputs to the lagoon. Similarly, the geoaccumulation index (Igeo) (Table 5, Supplementary Material; Fig. 3) showed non- to moderate contamination for Cd and up to high contamination for As and Sn. These patterns match the spatial and temporal variations detected identified through EF analysis.Fig. 2
Enrichment factor (EF) and categorization in sediments of Celestun lagoon, Yucatan, MexicoFig. 3
Geoaccumulation index in sediments of Celestun lagoon, Yucatan, Mexico

Ecological risk index (RI) values remained within the low-risk category for all elements, including Cd, despite its elevated concentrations relative to toxicity thresholds. This suggests that sediment characteristics such as pH, organic matter content, and grain size, may be limiting the mobility and bioavailability of these metals.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The consistent exceedance of SQuiRTs thresholds for As and Cd in all seasons underscores their role as persistent ecological stressors. In karstic environments such as Yucatan, alkaline pH conditions facilitate As mobilization (Sun et al. 2023), while the presence of interconnected sinkholes accelerates the transport of contaminants to coastal systems (Metcalfe et al. 2011). Intensive agrochemicals use further contributes to elevated Cd and As concentrations in groundwater and sediments (González Herrera 2018; López-Pacheco et al. 2019). These processes are exacerbated by the porous limestone geology, which enables rapid leaching of pollutants into the aquifer, posing risks not only to ecosystem integrity but also to human health, particularly in communities dependent on groundwater for drinking or cooking (Arcega-Cabrera and Fargher 2016).

The spatial and seasonal distribution of Ni, Zn, and Sn highlights the interaction between anthropogenic inputs and natural hydrological processes. Elevated Sn concentrations during the dry season are consistent with direct discharges from boat maintenance activities, while high Zn concentrations during the rainy season suggest enhanced influence from SGD and surface runoff. Seasonal enrichment of Al, Mn, As, and Sn during the dry season indicates that limited hydrological flushing promotes metal retention and sedimentation, facilitating their accumulation in surface sediments.

EF and Igeo analyses confirm chronic enrichment of Cd, As, and Sn in the lagoon, with particularly concerning levels of As and Sn during the dry season and across multiple sites. These findings point to a combination of localized sources and physicochemical conditions that promote metal accumulation and redistribution in sediments. Although the ecological risk index categorized the system as low risk, this likely reflects the mitigating effects of sediment properties on metal mobility rather than the absence of ecological or human health hazards.

Comparative studies in other karst coastal systems support these interpretations. Research has shown that Cd and As remain highly mobile and bioavailable in similar environments, leading to chronic exposure in benthic communities and bioaccumulation in higher trophic levels (Yu et al. 2022; El-Sharkawy et al. 2025). The presence of Sn, commonly introduced via antifouling paints, has been linked to endocrine disruption and reduced biodiversity in semi-enclosed lagoons with high boating activity (Zeng et al. 2024).

Taken together, these results suggest that while current ecological risk remains low, the persistent enrichment and bioavailability of Cd, As, and Sn represent a latent threat that could escalate under scenarios of intensified anthropogenic pressure or hydrological change. This underscores the urgent need for improved wastewater management, regulation of antifouling paint use, and continuous monitoring of metal concentrations to safeguard both ecosystem health and human well-being.

Mean metal concentrations in the dry, rainy and Nortes seasons are shown in Table 1 (Supplementary Material). These values were compared against the SQuiRTs thresholds (Buchman 2008) to assess potential damage to the early stages of the biota. Cd concentration exceeded these thresholds in all three seasons. Elevated Cd concentrations in groundwater have been previously reported by López-Pacheco et al. (2019) attributed to agrochemicals, untreated wastewater (Lian et al. 2024), and the burning of urban waste (common practice in the area—Arcega-Cabrera and Fargher 2016). According to the Secretariat of Agriculture and Rural Development (SADER 2022) Yucatan ranks 18th in fertilizer use among Mexican states. Given the karstic nature of the region’s soil, agrochemicals and their associated metal content can easily migrate into the aquifer and reach coastal ecosystems (González Herrera 2018).

Although the remaining metals were below the SQuiRTs threshold values, it is essential to evaluate their enrichment process, contamination levels, and most importantly the ecological risks these concentrations may pose to the CL system.

Spatial analysis (Table 2, Supplementary Material) revealed significant differences in chromium (Cr), copper (Cu), manganese (Mn), and nickel (Ni), with general higher concentrations observed from the central to the southern regions of the lagoon. These patterns suggest that metals inputs may be associated with urban wastewater discharge (Cañedo-López et al. 2014) and/or submarine groundwater discharges (SGD -Arcega-Cabrera et al. 2014; Kantún-Mazano et al. 2018).

Seasonal differences (Table 2, Supplementary Material) were significant for aluminum (Al), zinc (Zn), and tin (Sn). Al and Zn concentrations where higher during the rainy and Nortes seasons, while Sn exhibited high concentrations across all three seasons. The association with rainy and Nortes seasons suggests that these metals may originate from leaching processes in surrounding area (agrochemicals, urban settlements) and/or SGD (Suszek Goncalves et al. 2020; Kopczynski et al. 2025). In the case of Sn, continuous caulking of fishing and tourist boats in the area is a likely contributor (ATSDR 2005). Therefore, metal presence in the lagoon results from both local activities and inland sources transported via groundwater.

Enrichment factor (EF) values and their categorization (Table 4, Supplementary Material; Fig. 2) indicate minor to highly severe enrichment for As, Cd and Sn suggesting chronic input of these elements into the lagoon. Elevated Cd levels in groundwater have been previously reported (Polanco-Rodriguez et al. 2017), and the volume of SGD is sufficient to influence salinity gradients, implying that contaminant concentrations in these discharges may also be significant, although they remain unquantified. As and Sn exhibit even higher EF values and are distributed throughout most of the lagoon. As may also originate from SGD, as Arcega-Cabrera and Fargher (2016) reported its widespread use in the poultry industry, with bird feces commonly applied as organic fertilizer across Yucatan. Consequently, its presence in the aquifer and accumulation in the coastal lagoon sediments is unsurprising. Furthermore, karstic regions are particularly susceptible to As contamination due to alkaline pH conditions that enhance As mobility, and the presence of sinkholes facilitates rapid transport of contaminants from the surface to the aquifer (Sun et al. 2023). Sn is widely used in industrial, agricultural, and domestic applications (ATSDR 2005), and in the study area, it is also employed in boat maintenance, particularly in antifouling paints (Fujita et al. 2015; Telegdi et al. 2016).

Geoaccumulation index results and classifications are shown in Table 5 (Supplementary Material), with seasonal distributions shown in Fig. 3 for As, Cd and Sn. The index values range from non-contaminated to moderately and highly contaminated states for all three elements, with spatial and temporal patterns closely mirroring those observed in the EF analysis.

Ecological risk index (RI) values and classifications are shown in Table 6 (Supplementary Material). All elements were categorized as posing minor ecological risk, including Cd, despite its concentrations exceeding SQuiRTs thresholds. This outcome is unexpected given the observed enrichment and contamination levels. However, similar findings were reported by Hamid et al. (2022), where anthropogenic contamination was evident, yet ecological risk remained low to moderate due to sediment properties such as pH, grain size, organic carbon content amongst others, that reduce metal mobility and bioavailability.

Nonetheless, the enrichment and contamination levels of Cd, As and Sn remain concerning, particularly for sediment-dwelling and sediment-feeding organisms such as flamingos. Echeverría-García and Gold-Bouchot (2013) previously documented flamingo mortality in the area following hurricane Gilberto, attributed to ingestion of lead shot used in duck hunting that had become exposed in surface sediments. Benthonic biota is continuously exposed to these metals and serve as prey for fisheries and, in some cases, human consumption.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Celestun lagoon exhibits moderate to high levels of sediment contamination by As, Cd, and Sn, as evidenced by concentration data, enrichment factors, and geoaccumulation indices. These metals are primarily introduced through local anthropogenic activities, including wastewater discharge, boat maintenance, and agrochemical use, with additional contributions from submarine groundwater discharge.

Seasonal patterns indicate higher metal concentrations during the dry season, coinciding with reduced hydrological exchange and enhanced sedimentation. This supports the predominance of local sources over SGD as the main contributors during this period.

Although the ecological risk classifies the system as low risk, the persistent accumulation of metals in sediments and concentrations exceeding biological effect thresholds suggests potential long-term impacts on benthic communities and trophic networks. Current conditions facilitate chronic exposure scenarios, which may lead to bioaccumulation and pose health risks to wildlife and humans.

Monitoring and mitigation efforts should prioritize the regulation of local inputs, including the implementation of wastewater treatment infrastructure and stricter controls on port activities. Future research should focus on metal bioavailability, speciation and biomonitoring of exposed fauna to better assess ecological and human health risks in this karstic coastal system.

Celestun Lagoon is accumulating potentially toxic elements (As, Cd, and Sn) at concentrations and enrichment levels indicative of moderate to highly contaminated environment. While sediment characteristics such as pH and organic content may currently mitigate ecological risk, spatial and temporal variations point to both in situ and inland sources, particularly SGD and basin leaching as contributors to chronic metal enrichment. Coastal lagoon sediments are acting as sink for these contaminants, which may eventually pose a significant risk to environmental and human health. Therefore, wastewater treatment and solid waste management must be prioritized both inland and locally. The use of geochemical indeces alongside total concentration measurements is essential for accurately assessing potential risks to biota and human health.
